title: THE DEVIL DOESN’T NEED YOU TO REJECT THE BIBLE—HE ONLY NEEDS YOU TO BELIEVE A VERSE WITHOUT ITS CONTEXT
paragraphs: THE DEVIL DOESN’T NEED YOU TO REJECT THE BIBLE—HE ONLY NEEDS YOU TO BELIEVE A VERSE WITHOUT ITS CONTEXT
The most dangerous deception is not always a lie that sounds evil. Sometimes it is a Bible verse that sounds holy, quoted accurately, believed sincerely, and understood completely wrong.
What if I told you that one of the most frightening moments recorded in Scripture involved someone quoting the Bible perfectly—and using it to tempt Jesus Christ?
Not a pagan philosopher.
Not an atheist.
Not someone mocking the Word of God.
Satan himself.
And what makes that moment so disturbing is that the words he quoted were actually in Scripture.
He didn't need to invent a verse.
He only needed to misuse one.
Now think about that for a moment.
If the enemy was willing to quote Scripture to the Son of God, what makes us think he would hesitate to use Scripture against people who barely have time to read it?
That question should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Because somewhere today, a believer may be sharing a verse that God never intended to mean what the caption says.
Somewhere, a hurting person may be building their hope on a promise that was never given in the way they were taught.
Somewhere, a preacher may be using the Bible to strengthen his own authority rather than faithfully explain God's Word.
And somewhere, a sincere Christian may be confusing emotional excitement with spiritual understanding.
Not because they hate Jesus.
But because nobody taught them that a verse can be quoted correctly and interpreted dangerously.
And if we truly love Christ, we cannot afford to remain careless with the words He has given us.

The wilderness confrontation in Matthew 4 reveals something every believer needs to understand before another sermon, another viral Christian video, or another beautifully designed Scripture quotation crosses their screen.
Jesus had been fasting for forty days and forty nights.
He was hungry.
His body had endured genuine physical weakness.
And into that wilderness came the tempter.
First, Satan challenged Jesus to turn stones into bread. Jesus answered from Deuteronomy 8:3, declaring that human life depends not on bread alone but on every word proceeding from God.
Then the devil took Him to the pinnacle of the temple and challenged Him to throw Himself down.
And this time, Satan came armed with Scripture.
Matthew 4:6 records him quoting Psalm 91:
“He shall give his angels charge concerning thee.”
Then he continued with the promise that angels would bear Him up lest He strike His foot against a stone.
The quotation came from a real psalm about God's protection.
But Satan had turned a promise of divine care into an invitation to reckless presumption.
He wanted Jesus to manufacture a crisis and demand that the Father prove His faithfulness.
Jesus refused.
And His answer was devastatingly simple.
“Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” — Matthew 4:7, KJV
Jesus was quoting Deuteronomy 6:16.
He answered a misused Scripture with Scripture understood faithfully.
He did not deny Psalm 91.
He did not dismiss God's protection.
He rejected the devil's interpretation and application.
The original Greek of Matthew 4:7 reads:
Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου.
Ouk ekpeiraseis Kyrion ton Theon sou.
“You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
The verb ἐκπειράζω (ekpeirazō) carries the sense of putting someone to the test. In this context, Jesus refuses to turn trust in His Father into a demand for a spectacular demonstration.
And that distinction matters.
Faith trusts God's character.
Presumption attempts to force God's hand.
The devil tried to blur the difference by wrapping presumption in the language of Scripture.
That is why context is not an academic luxury. It is spiritual protection.
And the tragedy is that many believers have never been taught to recognize the difference.
Imagine a young woman sitting alone in her bedroom.
She has prayed for months.
Her marriage is falling apart.
Her finances are collapsing.
She is exhausted from pretending she is stronger than she feels.
Then she opens social media and sees Jeremiah 29:11.
“For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.”
For the first time that day, she smiles.
Someone has told her this means God will soon fix everything.
Her marriage will recover.
Her financial troubles will disappear.
Her next season will be easier.
And when none of those things happens, she begins asking a terrible question.
“Did God break His promise to me?”
But what if God never made the specific promise she was taught to expect?
What if the verse was beautiful, true, and genuinely encouraging—but its original meaning was different from the one attached to it?
Jeremiah 29 was written to Jewish exiles in Babylon.
They were living under judgment, displacement, and uncertainty.
False prophets were encouraging expectations of a quick resolution.
But through Jeremiah, God told the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, establish families, and seek the welfare of the city where they had been taken.
Why?
Because their exile would not end immediately.
Jeremiah 29:10 spoke of seventy years associated with Babylon's appointed period before the promised restoration.
Then came Jeremiah 29:11.
The promise was not originally a personalized guarantee that every individual believer would receive immediate prosperity.
It was God's assurance of His faithful purposes toward His covenant people amid a painful historical exile.
The Hebrew text contains these words:
מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה
Maḥshevot shalom velo lera'ah.
“Plans of peace/well-being and not for harm.”
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom) is richer than the modern idea of simply feeling peaceful. It can communicate welfare, wholeness, well-being, and peace.
But in Jeremiah's context, that promised welfare did not eliminate the reality of exile.
God's people still had to endure a long season they would never have chosen.
Do you see what changes when we read the whole passage?
The message is no longer, “God promises that nothing painful will happen to you.”
It becomes something far deeper.
God can remain faithful to His purposes even when His people must walk through suffering that does not end tomorrow.
That truth is not weaker.
It is stronger.
Because the believer whose prayers have not yet been answered needs more than a motivational slogan.
They need a God who remains faithful even when life refuses to become comfortable.
And that is exactly the kind of God Scripture reveals.
Maybe you have been there.
Maybe you believed that if you prayed hard enough, gave generously enough, served faithfully enough, and maintained enough faith, God would surely give you the outcome you wanted.
Then the diagnosis came.
The person you loved left.
The opportunity disappeared.
The child you prayed for continued struggling.
The miracle you expected never arrived.
And somewhere between disappointment and exhaustion, you started wondering whether your faith was defective.
But listen carefully.
A misunderstood promise can wound a sincere believer more deeply than an openly hostile argument against Christianity.
Because when a false expectation collapses, people sometimes blame the God who never authorized it.
That is why faithful Bible teaching is an act of love.
It protects wounded hearts from being crushed beneath promises Scripture never made.
And it protects the name of Jesus from being attached to claims He never taught.
The apostle Paul understood the danger.
In Acts 20:29–30, he warned the Ephesian elders that destructive influences would arise, including from among their own community, distorting the truth and drawing disciples away.
He was not merely concerned about people who openly rejected Christianity.
He was warning about deception that could emerge in religious environments.
That should sober us.
Not every person who speaks confidently about God speaks faithfully for God.
Not every emotional sermon is a sound sermon.
Not every miracle testimony proves that the theology surrounding it is correct.
Not every popular Christian teacher handles Scripture responsibly.
And not every interpretation that makes us feel powerful brings us closer to Christ.
The apostle John wrote:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
John was warning believers to test spiritual claims, especially in a setting where false prophets were active.
And how were Christians to test such claims?
Not by deciding whether a speaker sounded passionate enough.
Not by counting followers.
Not by measuring how many people cried during the message.
But by discerning whether the teaching faithfully confessed the truth about Jesus Christ and remained consistent with apostolic teaching.
Truth is not established by volume.
A trembling voice can tell the truth.
A confident voice can spread error.
And a sermon can bring thousands of people to tears while leaving them with a distorted understanding of God.
That does not mean emotions are wrong.
Jesus wept.
Paul spoke with tears.
The Psalms are filled with anguish, gratitude, fear, longing, and praise.
Biblical faith is not emotionally lifeless.
But emotion must respond to truth, not replace it.
The Holy Spirit does not need us to distort Scripture to make God's Word powerful.
Consider another passage that is frequently misunderstood.
Philippians 4:13.
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”
Beautiful words.
Powerful words.
But what did Paul mean?
Was he claiming that Christians can achieve absolutely anything they imagine?
That every business venture will succeed?
That every ambition is guaranteed?
That faith makes failure impossible?
Read the verses before it.
Paul said he knew how to be brought low and how to abound.
He knew hunger.
He knew abundance.
He knew need.
He knew plenty.
And in that context, he declared that he could endure all these circumstances through the One who strengthened him.
The Greek says:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με.
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
A close rendering is:
“I have strength for all things in the one who strengthens me.”
In context, “all things” refers to the varied circumstances Paul had just described.
He was not presenting Jesus as a guarantee of unlimited personal achievement.
He was testifying to Christ's sufficiency in both abundance and deprivation.
And suddenly, the verse becomes even more extraordinary.
Because the Christian who lost the job can still say it.
The mother caring for a seriously ill child can still say it.
The elderly believer whose body is weakening can still say it.
The persecuted disciple can still say it.
The person who has nothing left except Christ can still say it.
Not because Jesus guarantees that every circumstance will become favorable.
But because Christ can strengthen His people to remain faithful when their circumstances are not.
That is not motivational thinking.
That is Gospel-rooted endurance.
And it is exactly the kind of truth that survives when inspirational slogans fall apart.
Now imagine what happens when Scripture is mishandled not merely to encourage people, but to control them.
Someone tells a struggling believer, “Touch not mine anointed.”
They quote Psalm 105:15.
Then they insist that questioning a pastor's teaching is equivalent to rebelling against God.
A sincere Christian becomes afraid to ask questions.
Afraid to examine financial practices.
Afraid to compare sermons with Scripture.
Afraid to speak when something appears wrong.
But read Psalm 105 in context.
The passage recounts God's protection of the patriarchs during their vulnerable journeys, when they were few in number and living among other nations.
It is not a universal exemption placing modern religious leaders beyond examination or accountability.
In fact, the New Testament instructs believers to test teaching.
Paul publicly confronted Peter when Peter's conduct was inconsistent with the truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
And the Bereans were commended for examining the Scriptures to determine whether Paul's message was true.
Acts 17:11 says they:
“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.”
Think about that.
They examined the teaching of an apostle.
And Scripture calls their response noble.
They were not condemned for checking.
They were commended.
The Greek word describing their examination is connected to ἀνακρίνω (anakrinō), meaning to examine, investigate, or evaluate.
Their faith was not mindless acceptance.
It was receptive, diligent examination.
They listened eagerly.
And they searched carefully.
Those two actions belonged together.
A faithful teacher should not be threatened when Christians open their Bibles.
A faithful pastor does not need to replace your conscience.
A faithful ministry does not need to make you afraid of honest questions.
A faithful disciple does not treat every disagreement as persecution.
Because the goal of Christian teaching is not to create dependence on a human personality.
It is to lead people into mature faithfulness to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus is not threatened by truth.
He is the truth.
But there is another danger.
One that can hide inside those of us who genuinely care about biblical accuracy.
We can become so determined to correct everyone else's interpretation that we forget to let Scripture correct our own hearts.
We learn the Greek words.
We study Hebrew grammar.
We memorize historical timelines.
We recognize false teaching.
We can explain covenant theology, literary genres, and the difference between descriptive and prescriptive passages.
And still become proud.
Still refuse to forgive.
Still mistreat our families.
Still look down on believers who know less than we do.
Still use truth like a weapon against people we were commanded to love.
That is not spiritual maturity.
That is knowledge disconnected from obedience.
Paul warned in 1 Corinthians 8:1:
“Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.”
In its context, Paul was addressing knowledge and love in the dispute concerning food offered to idols.
His warning remains relevant whenever Christians allow knowledge to inflate their sense of superiority rather than strengthen their love for others.
Biblical context matters.
But the purpose of understanding Scripture is not to win every argument.
It is to know God truthfully, worship Him faithfully, obey Him humbly, and love others rightly.
We must never confuse accurate interpretation with automatic spiritual transformation.
The Pharisees knew the Scriptures.
Many were deeply committed to studying and preserving the biblical text.
Yet Jesus confronted those who failed to recognize what the Scriptures revealed about Him.
In John 5:39–40, Jesus said:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.”
Here is the heartbreak.
People could be devoted to Scripture and still resist the Savior to whom Scripture pointed.
They could know the words and miss the Word made flesh.
They could study divine promises while rejecting their fulfillment in Christ.
And that warning belongs to us, too.
Because the ultimate goal of biblical interpretation is not merely to understand ancient documents.
It is to understand the revelation of God that finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Luke 24 records the risen Jesus walking with two disciples on the road to Emmaus.
They were grieving.
Confused.
Disappointed.
They had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel.
But He had been crucified.
Their expectations had collapsed.
And they did not yet understand the meaning of what had happened.
Jesus did something extraordinary.
He did not simply offer them an inspirational message.
He explained the Scriptures.
Beginning with Moses and the Prophets, He interpreted the things concerning Himself.
Luke 24:27 describes Him:
“He expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.”
The Greek verb διερμήνευσεν (diermēneusen) means that He explained or interpreted.
The risen Christ helped them understand the biblical story in light of His suffering and glory.
And later they said:
“Did not our heart burn within us... while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Luke 24:32).
Notice the order.
Christ opened the Scriptures.
And their hearts burned.
Their hearts were not warmed by a distortion.
They were moved by truth.
They did not need the Word of God to be made more dramatic through manipulation.
They needed their eyes opened to what God had actually revealed.
That is the kind of encounter with Scripture we desperately need today.
Not less passion.
More truth.
Not less conviction.
Deeper understanding.
Not less dependence on the Holy Spirit.
More willingness to submit our assumptions to the Word He inspired.
And above everything else, more of Jesus.
Because when the Bible is interpreted faithfully, we begin to see a story far greater than ourselves.
A story that begins with creation.
Moves through humanity's rebellion.
Reveals God's holiness and covenant faithfulness.
Exposes the terrible reality of sin.
Unfolds God's promises.
And reaches its decisive fulfillment in the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
This is where context becomes more than protection against false teaching.
It becomes a doorway into the wonder of the Gospel.
Think about the scandal of the cross.
The sinless Son of God condemned.
The Holy One mocked.
The Creator rejected by His creatures.
The Messiah crucified like a criminal.
To the watching world, it looked like humiliation and defeat.
But Scripture reveals something infinitely greater.
Isaiah 53 speaks of the suffering servant bearing the sins of many.
Jesus taught that the Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
Paul proclaimed that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The cross was not evidence that God's redemptive purpose had failed.
It was central to its fulfillment.
And the resurrection was God's victorious vindication of His Son.
What looked like the end was not the end.
What appeared to be shame became the place where God's grace was gloriously displayed.
What seemed like darkness could not overcome the Light.
Not because He changes God's truth to fit our preferences.
But because His redeeming work changes the destiny of sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
And maybe that is the part of this article you needed most.
Perhaps you have been deceived.
Perhaps you trusted someone who used God's name to manipulate you.
Perhaps you believed a teaching that left you spiritually exhausted.
Perhaps you gave money because someone told you God would punish you if you refused.
Perhaps you stayed silent when you should have asked questions.
Perhaps you walked away from a church because you could no longer distinguish between the voice of Christ and the demands of people claiming to represent Him.
Or perhaps you have been the person who shared misleading verses.
The person who repeated a sermon without checking it.
The person who taught something confidently and later discovered it was wrong.
If that is you, hear this.
Being corrected by Scripture is not the end of your faith. It can be the beginning of deeper faithfulness.
You do not need to defend every interpretation you have ever believed.
You do not need to pretend you have never misunderstood God.
You do not need to protect your reputation at the expense of truth.
You can repent.
You can learn.
You can grow.
You can ask forgiveness where your teaching or actions have harmed others.
And you can return to Christ.
Because the Gospel does not announce salvation for people who have always understood everything correctly.
It announces salvation through Jesus Christ for sinners who need mercy.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast.
Even our theological knowledge cannot purchase redemption.
We are not justified by mastering Greek.
We are not reconciled to God by winning doctrinal debates.
We are not forgiven because we can explain every difficult passage.
We are saved through the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
And that grace does not make truth unnecessary.
It teaches us to love truth without making ourselves the center of it.
So how do we protect ourselves?
We begin with a humble question.
“What did God actually mean when this was written?”
Before asking what a verse means to me, I need to ask what it meant in its original setting.
Who wrote it?
To whom?
Under what circumstances?
What comes before it?
What follows it?
Is this poetry, prophecy, historical narrative, wisdom literature, a parable, or an apostolic letter?
Is the passage describing what happened, or commanding what should happen?
Is this a promise to a particular person or people, a general principle, or a teaching applicable to all believers?
How does it fit within the whole counsel of Scripture?
And how does it relate to the person and work of Jesus Christ without forcing Him artificially into details the passage does not support?
These are not questions reserved for seminary professors.
They are questions for ordinary Christians who love God's Word enough to handle it carefully.
You do not need to know Hebrew or Greek to begin reading responsibly.
Faithful translations, careful reading, trustworthy teachers, prayer, and a willingness to examine whole passages can take you far.
The original languages can illuminate meaning, but isolated Greek or Hebrew words must also be interpreted in their sentences, literary contexts, and historical settings.
A dramatic word study is not automatically a faithful interpretation.
And a person who quotes the original language is not automatically correct.
Humility matters.
Patience matters.
The surrounding passage matters.
The entire biblical witness matters.
And above all, Christ matters.
Paul wrote in 2 Timothy 2:15:
“Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.”
The Greek expression translated “rightly dividing” is ὀρθοτομοῦντα (orthotomounta).
It conveys the idea of handling or guiding something correctly—here, the word of truth.
The point is not to invent hidden meanings or divide Scripture arbitrarily.
It is to handle God's message faithfully.
And that requires more than repeating what we have heard.
It requires responsibility.
Because Scripture is not ours to manipulate.
It is God's Word to receive, understand, believe, and obey.
Imagine what could happen if Christians began taking this seriously.
Imagine parents reading entire Bible passages with their children rather than only repeating isolated inspirational quotations.
Imagine young believers learning to recognize when someone twists Scripture to pressure them.
Imagine churches where pastors welcome thoughtful questions because their authority is accountable to God's Word.
Imagine Christians who are passionate about sound doctrine and equally passionate about mercy.
Imagine believers who can disagree without cruelty, correct without humiliation, and defend truth without forgetting the people Jesus came to save.
Imagine fewer wounded souls abandoning Christianity because someone sold them a false version of God's promises.
Imagine more disciples whose faith is strong enough to endure suffering because it was built on what Christ actually taught.
That is worth working toward.
And that is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your Bible.
Not to become the voice you follow without examination.
But to encourage deeper engagement with Scripture, more faithful discipleship, greater spiritual discernment, and a life increasingly centered on Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, strengthen their walk with Christ, and continue learning beyond a single article or sermon.
Read.
Compare what you learn with the Bible.
Ask questions.
Share what is helpful.
And remember that no library, ministry, or teacher is beyond the need for biblical examination.
We want people who love Jesus more than they love a platform.
People who treasure Scripture more than slogans.
People whose convictions become deeper because their understanding becomes more faithful.
And if this mission speaks to your heart, there is another way you can participate.
For those who are able and willing, it is a practical way to participate financially in a ministry effort you believe is worth sustaining.
Scripture does encourage generous support for Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 teaches that those instructed in the Word should share good things with those who teach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion.
That distinction is essential.
Think of it as a recurring offering toward a mission you want to see continue.
Not a purchase of spiritual blessing.
Not a transaction with God.
But a willing contribution toward the work of sharing biblical teaching and discipleship resources.
Those items are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
Your prayers, your faithful witness, and your willingness to share biblical truth matter too.
Someone may be struggling under a false promise.
Someone may be afraid to question a teaching that has harmed them.
Someone may be quietly wondering whether Jesus is still trustworthy after being disappointed by people who claimed to speak for Him.
And perhaps this article could encourage them to open their Bible again.
Not every share will change someone's life.
But every thoughtful share creates another opportunity for truth to be encountered.

If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them—not to embarrass them, correct them publicly, or imply they are deceived, but because you believe they would genuinely benefit from the message.
And I want to ask you something personal.
Not for an argument.
Not for a performance of spirituality.
But for an honest conversation among people who are still learning to follow Jesus.
Have you ever discovered that a Bible verse you believed for years meant something different when you finally read it in context?
What changed?
Did it strengthen your faith?
Did it challenge something you had been taught?
Did it help you understand God more clearly?
Your testimony might help another believer find the courage to examine a teaching they have been afraid to question.
Or perhaps you are in a different place.
Perhaps you are realizing that you have been repeating religious ideas without checking whether they were biblical.
Perhaps you are exhausted from trying to make God's promises fit the life you expected.
Perhaps you simply want to begin again, with an open Bible and a humble heart.
Not because those words are a formula.
Not because commenting proves your faith.
But because sometimes an honest confession becomes the beginning of a meaningful conversation and a renewed commitment to seek God.
You do not have to disclose private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
And if you know someone who has been hurt by distorted teaching, please approach them with compassion.
They may not need another heated debate.
They may need someone patient enough to listen, open Scripture with them, and remind them that Jesus Christ is not the same as every person who has misrepresented Him.
Because our greatest desire should never be to build a large audience that agrees with everything we say.
It should be to see people become faithful disciples of the Lord Jesus Christ.
People who know the Gospel.
People who recognize deception.
People who repent when confronted by truth.
People who extend grace because they have received grace.
People who understand that Scripture is not a collection of inspirational phrases waiting to be detached from their meaning.
It is God's revelation, given through real authors, in real historical circumstances, with words that deserve to be understood faithfully.
And it ultimately directs us to the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
One day, every viral sermon will be forgotten.
Every social media trend will disappear.
Every platform will lose its importance.
Every human teacher will be shown to have limitations.
But the truth of God's Word will not lose its authority.
Jesus declared in Matthew 24:35:
“Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.”
So do not build your faith on the most persuasive voice in the room.
Do not surrender your discernment to the most popular preacher on your screen.
Do not confuse a beautiful quotation with a faithful interpretation.
And do not allow fear of being corrected to keep you from discovering what Scripture actually says.
Open the Bible.
Read the whole passage.
Seek wise and accountable teaching.
Pray for understanding.
Test what you hear.
Repent when you are wrong.
Hold fast to what is true.
And keep your eyes on Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest danger is not simply that someone might persuade you to believe something false about a Bible verse.
It is that a distorted understanding of Scripture might lead you to misunderstand the character of the God who loved sinners enough to send His Son.
And the greatest gift of faithful interpretation is not intellectual superiority.
It is seeing more clearly the holiness, mercy, faithfulness, and saving grace of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who resisted Satan's misuse of Scripture in the wilderness is the Savior who gave Himself for our sins.
The same Jesus who opened the Scriptures on the road to Emmaus is the risen Lord who calls people to repentance and faith.
And the same Jesus who confronted religious hypocrisy is the gracious Redeemer who receives those who come to Him.
You do not have to remain trapped in spiritual confusion.
You do not have to keep defending what you now recognize was wrong.
You do not have to pretend your past mistakes are stronger than His mercy.
Come to Christ.
Bring your questions.
Bring your failures.
Bring the teachings you need to examine.
Bring the shame you have been carrying.
And let His Word correct what is false, strengthen what is weak, and direct your heart toward the truth.
Because the God who calls us out of darkness does not invite us into another kind of blindness.
He calls us to walk in the light of His Son.
Never let someone use a verse to lead you away from the Savior the whole Scripture was given to reveal.
